| *Play havoc with* | cause great disorder or damage to |
| *Bear the palm* | win the first prize or highest honour |

**People and character**

| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *An Achilles' heel* | one weak point in an otherwise strong person or system |
| *A man of straw* | a person of no substance or influence |
| *A man of letters* | a learned writer or scholar |
| *A man of his word* | one who always keeps his promises |
| *A fair-weather friend* | a friend who disappears in your bad days |
| *A snake in the grass* | a treacherous enemy hiding as a friend |
| *A wolf in sheep's clothing* | a dangerous person disguised as harmless |
| *Odd man out* | the one member unlike all the others |
| *A cog in the machine* | an insignificant worker in a vast system |
| *A tower of strength* | a person who gives firm support in crisis |
| *A jack of all trades* | one who does many kinds of work, master of none |
| *Have a finger in every pie* | meddle in everyone's business |
| *Wear your heart on your sleeve* | display your feelings openly |
| *Keep your chin up* | stay brave and cheerful in hardship |
| *Keep the wolf from the door* | earn just enough to avoid hunger |
| *Keep body and soul together* | barely manage to survive |
| *Take someone to task* | scold or criticise someone severely |
| *Be all ears* | listen with complete eagerness |
| *Be in two minds* | be unable to decide between options |
| *Sit on the fence* | avoid taking sides in a dispute |
| *Keep your fingers crossed* | hope anxiously that things will go well |
| *Break the ice* | start conversation among strangers |
| *Hit the nail on the head* | describe a situation with exact correctness |
| *A foregone conclusion* | a result obvious in advance |
| *At daggers drawn* | in open, bitter hostility |
| *In the doldrums* | low in spirits or activity |
| *Not mince matters* | speak plainly without softening words |
| *Take to task* | reprimand for a fault |

**Situation families:** trouble (in hot water, in a pickle, in the doldrums), effort (move heaven and earth, leave no stone unturned, burn the midnight oil), suddenness (a bolt from the blue, out of the blue, at the drop of a hat, on the spur of the moment, off and on is the exception — irregularity), defeat and quitting (throw in the towel, bite the dust, get the sack, end in smoke), improvement (turn over a new leaf, bury the hatchet), blame-shifting (pass the buck, steal a march, turn the tables).

**People families:** the weak (man of straw, cog in the machine), the treacherous (snake in the grass, wolf in sheep's clothing, fair-weather friend), the reliable (man of his word, tower of strength, salt of the earth), the mixed-ability (jack of all trades), the famous weak-spot (Achilles' heel).

Cluster-learning pays double here: when the stem says 'a sudden and unexpected event', the whole suddenness family surfaces, and the options — usually drawn one per family — separate instantly.

tricks.title: Family surfacing
tricks.body: Classify the stem's demand: sudden? trouble? effort? defeat? person-type? Recall the family's four members; the right one is usually among the options, and the wrong options are from *other* families.

tricks.title: Allusion anchors
tricks.body: A few idioms hide a story: Achilles' heel (the hero's one weak spot), bell the cat (the mouse that dared), pass the buck (shifting the deal-marker). One-line stories fix meanings permanently.

tricks.title: Outcome test
tricks.body: For action idioms, ask what changes at the end: throw in the towel → the fight stops (give up); turn the tables → positions reverse; face the music → consequences arrive.

mistakes: Reading 'steal a march' as theft — it means to gain a secret advantage.
Taking 'pass the buck' as giving money; the buck is the marker of responsibility.
Confusing 'in the doldrums' (depressed/inactive) with 'in the dumps' — same sense, but options plant 'a boring place'.
Reading 'against all odds' as 'very unfair odds' instead of 'despite difficulties'.
subtopics.notes:
### Two big groups
Most idioms in competitive exams fall into two groups:
1. **Situation idioms** — they describe what is happening: trouble, hard work, sudden events, success, defeat.
2. **People idioms** — they describe a type of person: loyal, false, weak, skilled, clever.

If you know which group and which family an idiom belongs to, the right option stands out.

### Situation families
| Family | Idioms | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Trouble | in hot water, in a fix, in deep waters | in serious difficulty |
| Hard effort | burn the midnight oil, leave no stone unturned, move heaven and earth | work very hard / try every way |
| Sudden | at the drop of a hat, on the spur of the moment | at once / without planning |
| Money | make both ends meet, keep the wolf from the door | manage with little income |
| Change | turn over a new leaf, turn the tables | start behaving better / reverse the position |
| Winning | carry the day, bear the palm | win |
| Losing, quitting | throw in the towel, bite the dust, take to one's heels | give up / be defeated / run away |
| Health, mood | under the weather, on cloud nine | slightly ill / extremely happy |

Worked use: *The police left no stone unturned to find the child.* Effort family → **tried every possible way**.

### People families
| Type | Idioms | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| False friend | a snake in the grass, a fair-weather friend, a wolf in sheep's clothing | hidden enemy / friend only in good times / harmful person who looks harmless |
| Weak or unimportant | a man of straw, a cog in the machine | person of no real power |
| Reliable | a man of his word, a tower of strength | keeps promises / gives strong support |
| Many skills | a jack of all trades | does many jobs, masters none |
| Second place | play second fiddle | take a less important role |

### Idioms from stories (allusions)
Some idioms come from old stories. One line of the story fixes the meaning for ever.
- **Achilles' heel** — a Greek hero could be hurt only at his heel → a weak point.
- **Bell the cat** — the mice wanted a bell on the cat, but none dared tie it → to take a big risk for everyone.
- **Pandora's box** — opening a forbidden box let out all troubles → a source of many new problems.
- **A Herculean task** — Hercules did twelve very hard labours → a task needing huge effort.
- **Midas touch** — whatever King Midas touched became gold → the ability to make money from anything.
- **A Trojan horse** — soldiers hid inside a wooden horse gifted to Troy → something harmless-looking that harms from inside.

### Fill-in-the-blank type
Read the sentence and name the family it needs. *Seeing the police, the thief ___.* The thief wants to escape → running away → **took to his heels**. Then read the sentence again with your choice.

### Common traps
- *Steal a march on* is not stealing; it means gaining an advantage quietly.
- *Pass the buck* is not about money; it means shifting blame.
- *Play second fiddle* is not about music; it means a lower role.
- *Under the weather* is not about rain; it means slightly ill.

### Quick revision
- Name the family first: trouble, effort, sudden, money, change, win, lose, health.
- People idioms: false (snake, fair-weather), weak (straw, cog), reliable (word, tower).
- Story idioms: Achilles' heel, bell the cat, Pandora's box, Herculean, Midas touch, Trojan horse.
- In blanks, match the family the sentence needs.

patterns.name: Meaning of a situation idiom
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom describes an event or condition: trouble, effort, suddenness, winning, losing, health.
patterns.logic:
1. Place the idiom in its family (effort, trouble, sudden...).
2. Reject options from other families and literal options.
3. Pick the option that states the family meaning exactly.

*Why it works:* distractors are usually taken from other families.

example.q: Meaning of *By leaps and bounds*: (a) very rapidly (b) by jumping (c) with great fear (d) slowly and steadily
example.solution: Leaps = big fast jumps → speed. Answer: **(a) very rapidly**.

patterns.name: Meaning of a people (character) idiom
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom names a type of person: 'a ___ friend', 'a man of ___', 'a ___ in the grass'.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide whether the idiom praises or criticises the person.
2. Recall the type: false, weak, reliable, many-skilled.
3. Choose the option with that type.

*Why it works:* people idioms are labels; the label's tone removes half the options.

example.q: Meaning of *A jack of all trades*: (a) a skilled mechanic (b) one who does many kinds of work but masters none (c) a rich trader (d) a lazy worker
example.solution: The full saying ends 'master of none'. Answer: **(b)**.

patterns.name: Fill the blank with the right situation idiom
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence with a blank and four idioms as options.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the sentence and name what is needed (run away? lower role? try harder?).
2. Match the family.
3. Re-read with the chosen idiom; check tense and grammar.

*Why it works:* the context supports only one meaning.

example.q: *Having won one medal, the athlete did not ___; she trained even harder.* (a) rest on her laurels (b) burn her boats (c) play to the gallery (d) break the ice
example.solution: She kept working instead of relaxing after success → **(a) rest on her laurels** (be satisfied with past success).

patterns.name: Idioms from stories and legends
patterns.howToSpot: A proper noun or story object appears: Achilles, Pandora, Hercules, Midas, Trojan, a cat with a bell.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the one-line story.
2. Turn the story's key point into a general meaning.
3. Reject literal options about the story's objects.

*Why it works:* the story is the meaning; options that retell it literally are wrong.

example.q: Meaning of *The Midas touch*: (a) a gentle touch (b) the ability to make money from anything one does (c) a royal order (d) a golden ornament
example.solution: Everything Midas touched turned to gold. Answer: **(b)**.

subtopics.title: Phrasal verbs (verb + particle phrases)
subtopics.concept: A **phrasal verb** is a verb joined with a small word (a particle) such as *up, off, out, in, after, down*. Together they make a new meaning: *give* + *up* = stop doing something. Idiom sections and fill-in-the-blank questions often test these phrases.

tricks.title: Particle meanings
tricks.body: *off* often means stop or cancel (call off, put off); *out* means finish or remove (run out, put out); *up* means complete or give up; *after* means follow or care for (look after, take after).

tricks.title: Same verb, four particles
tricks.body: When all four options share one verb (break down / out / up / in), say the sentence with each and keep the one whose meaning fits the whole sentence.

tricks.title: One-word swap
tricks.body: Replace the phrasal verb with a single formal word to check it: put out = extinguish, call off = cancel, put up with = tolerate, come across = meet by chance.

mistakes: Guessing from the verb alone: *give in* (surrender) and *give up* (stop a habit) differ only in the particle.
Mixing *put off* (postpone) with *put out* (extinguish).
Reading *look down upon* literally as looking from a height; it means to think someone is inferior.
Using *look after* (take care of) where *look into* (investigate) is needed.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a phrasal verb?
A **phrasal verb** is a verb + a small word called a **particle** (up, off, out, in, on, down, after, into, over). Together they give a new meaning that you often cannot guess from the verb alone.
- *give* = hand over, but *give up* = stop doing something.
- *call* = phone or shout, but *call off* = cancel.

In competitive exams they appear in three places: the idioms-and-phrases question ('meaning of the phrase *put up with*'), fill-in-the-blank ('The meeting was put ___'), and error spotting or sentence improvement.

### What the particles usually mean
The particle is the key. These are tendencies, not strict rules, but they help a lot.

| Particle | Usual idea | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| off | stop, cancel, leave | call off (cancel), put off (postpone), take off (plane leaves the ground) |
| out | finish, remove, appear | run out of (finish), put out (extinguish), break out (start suddenly) |
| up | complete, stop, arrive | give up (stop a habit), turn up (arrive), bring up (raise a child) |
| down | reduce, fail, refuse | break down (stop working), turn down (refuse), look down upon (despise) |
| in | enter, yield | give in (surrender), hand in (submit), break in (enter by force) |
| after | follow, care | look after (take care of), take after (resemble an elder) |
| into | examine, meet | look into (investigate), run into (meet by chance) |
| over | recover, examine | get over (recover from), look over (check quickly) |

### One verb, many meanings
Examiners like to fix one verb and change the particle.

| Verb | + particle | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| give | up / in / away / out | stop a habit / surrender / donate or reveal / distribute or run short |
| turn | down / up / out | refuse / arrive / prove to be |
| take | after / off / up | resemble / remove or leave the ground / start a hobby |
| break | down / out / in / up | stop working / start suddenly / enter by force / end a relationship |
| come | across / about | meet by chance / happen |
| put | off / out / up with | postpone / extinguish / tolerate |

Worked use: *The car broke ___ on the highway.* Cars stop working → **broke down**. *Broke out* is for war, fire or disease. *Broke in* is for thieves.

### Three-word phrasal verbs
Some phrasal verbs have two particles and must stay together: *put up with* (tolerate), *run out of* (have none left), *look down upon* (despise), *look forward to* (wait eagerly). Do not drop the second particle: 'We have run out sugar' is wrong; say 'run out **of** sugar'.

### How to answer
1. **Meaning questions:** replace the phrasal verb with a one-word meaning (cancel, tolerate, extinguish) and test it in a sentence.
2. **Particle blanks:** read the whole sentence. The subject (a car, a fire, a meeting) tells you which particle makes sense.
3. **Replace-the-word questions:** the bold word is formal (extinguish, postpone, recover); find the phrasal verb that equals it.

### Quick revision
- off = cancel/stop; out = finish/remove; up = stop/arrive; down = refuse/fail; after = care/resemble; into = investigate.
- call off = cancel; put off = postpone; put out = extinguish; put up with = tolerate.
- give up = stop a habit; give in = surrender; turn down = refuse; take after = resemble.
- break down = stop working; break out = start suddenly; come across = meet by chance; get over = recover.

patterns.name: Meaning of a phrasal verb
patterns.howToSpot: A phrase like 'to call off' or 'to put up with' is given as the idiom/phrase; options are one-word or short meanings.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the particle's idea (off = stop/cancel).
2. Replace the phrase with each option in a small sentence.
3. Reject options that use the verb's plain meaning (call = phone).

*Why it works:* the particle changes the verb's meaning, and the plain-verb option is the planted trap.

example.q: Meaning of *To bring up*: (a) to lift something (b) to raise and educate a child (c) to carry upstairs (d) to arrive early
example.solution: *Bring up* a child = raise the child. Answer: **(b)**.

patterns.name: Fill in the particle
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence with a blank right after a verb; options are particles (off, on, up, out, down, in).
patterns.logic:
1. Find the subject and object (a car, a fire, sugar).
2. Say the sentence with each particle.
3. Keep the only one that makes sense for that subject.

*Why it works:* each verb + particle pair has a fixed meaning; the subject allows only one.

example.q: *The students were asked to hand ___ their answer sheets.* (a) in (b) on (c) off (d) up
example.solution: *Hand in* = submit. Answer: **(a) in**.

patterns.name: Same verb, different particles
patterns.howToSpot: All four options share one verb (give up / give in / give away / give out) and a meaning is asked for.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall what each particle adds to the verb.
2. Match the given meaning exactly.
3. Beware of a close pair (give up vs give in).

*Why it works:* only the particle changes, so knowing particle ideas separates the options.

example.q: Select the phrasal verb that means *to meet by chance*: (a) run into (b) run out (c) run over (d) run away
example.solution: *Run into* someone = meet by chance. Answer: **(a)**.

patterns.name: Replace a word with a phrasal verb
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a formal verb in bold (extinguish, recover, postpone); options are phrasal verbs.
patterns.logic:
1. Keep the bold word's meaning in mind.
2. Test each phrasal verb in its place.
3. Watch the tense: the option must match (got over, not get over, in a past sentence).

*Why it works:* each formal word has one common phrasal-verb equal.

example.q: Replace the bold word: *The plane **departed** at 6 a.m.* (a) took off (b) took up (c) took after (d) took in
example.solution: Planes *take off* = leave the ground. Answer: **(a) took off**.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy: banking 300 idioms in 30 days
subtopics.concept:
Tier 1 carries exactly one idiom item in most shifts; Tier 2 occasionally uses idioms inside cloze and RC. The topic is pure bank-and-recall, and a 300-idiom working bank covers years of papers.

**The 30-day plan:**
- **Days 1–10:** 10 new idioms a day from the banks in this topic, each used in one sentence of your own. Sentence-production is what survives exam pressure; recognition alone melts.
- **Days 11–20:** 10 new + 15 old daily. Group by family (animals, colours, situations) — clusters recall better than alphabetical lists.
- **Days 21–30:** 10 new + 25 old + one 20-item mixed self-test. Anything failed twice goes onto a separate 'bleeder list' of 15–20 items that gets one extra revision weekly.

**In the exam:** 20 seconds. Kill literal options, translate the picture, plug back. If unknown, judge polarity (does it sound positive?) and pick the same-polarity option — instinct on familiar-sounding idioms is right far more than chance.

**Total time budget for the whole topic: about 5 hours spread over a month** — the best time-to-mark ratio in the English section, provided sentences are produced and the bleeder list exists. Do not chase exhaustive dictionaries; the SSC idiom pool is surprisingly small and heavily recycled.

tricks.title: Sentence production
tricks.body: For every idiom, speak a sentence about your own life ('I burned the midnight oil before my SSC mock'). Personal sentences are recalled under pressure; list-readings are not.

tricks.title: Family-first revision
tricks.body: Revise by bank (animals → body → colours → food → situations → people). Each bank is one mental room; in the exam you 'enter the room' and the members appear.

tricks.title: Bleeder list
tricks.body: Fail an idiom twice in self-tests? It goes to a 15-item list revised weekly. Most permanent marks come from this list, not from new words.

mistakes: Learning idioms as word-pairs without ever producing a sentence.
Revising alphabetically; families and pairs are the recall units.
Chasing rare literary idioms — SSC recycles a small common pool.
Ignoring tone: options often mix one positive and three negative meanings, or vice versa.
subtopics.notes:
### How idioms appear in the paper
Idioms are a small but steady part of the English section. Most papers ask one or two direct idiom questions. Idioms also hide inside cloze tests, sentence improvement and fill-in-the-blank items. The pool of idioms examiners use is small and repeats often, so a well-built list of about 300 idioms covers most of what you will see.

### The different formats
1. **Meaning of the idiom** — one idiom, four meanings. The most common.
2. **Replace the phrase** — a sentence has a plain phrase underlined; you choose the idiom that can replace it. *'They are in bitter open hostility'* → *'They are at daggers drawn'*.
3. **Complete the idiom** — one word of a fixed idiom is missing: *calls a spade a ___*. Idioms are frozen, so only the original word is correct. 'A spade a shovel' is simply wrong.
4. **Opposite meaning** — choose the option opposite to the idiom's meaning. First find the meaning, then find its opposite. The option that gives the same meaning is the trap.
5. **Idiom inside a passage** — the context gives it away.

### Idioms are frozen
You cannot change the words of an idiom. *A hard nut to crack*, never *a hard nut to break*. *Every cloud has a silver lining*, never *a golden lining*. This is why the 'complete the idiom' type has only one defensible answer. When you learn an idiom, learn its exact words.

### A 30-day plan
- **Days 1–10:** learn 10 new idioms a day. For each, make one sentence about your own life: *I burnt the midnight oil before my mock test.*
- **Days 11–20:** 10 new + revise 15 old each day. Revise by family (animals, body, colours, food, situations, people).
- **Days 21–30:** 10 new + revise 25 old + a 20-question self-test. Any idiom you get wrong twice goes on a short **weak list**. Revise that list every week.

Your own sentence is what you remember in the exam. Reading a list alone fades fast.

### In the exam hall (20 seconds per idiom)
1. Kill the literal option.
2. Find the picture and the family.
3. Check the tone: positive or negative?
4. Plug the answer back into a sentence.

If you do not know the idiom at all, judge its tone from the key words and pick the option with the same tone. This beats a blind guess.

### Opposite-meaning questions
Write the meaning in two words first. *Keep one's chin up* = stay cheerful. Now the opposite is *lose heart*. The option that says 'stay brave' has the **same** meaning and is the planted trap.

### Quick revision
| Format | First step |
|---|---|
| Meaning | Kill the literal option |
| Replace the phrase | Find the idiom with exactly that meaning |
| Complete the idiom | Recall the frozen original word |
| Opposite | Write the meaning, then reverse it |
| In a passage | Use the situation to fix the tone |

- 10 new idioms a day, one own sentence each, weekly weak list.
- Idioms are frozen: never accept a changed word.

patterns.name: Complete the idiom (missing word)
patterns.howToSpot: An idiom appears with one word blanked, and the options are four similar words (spade/shovel, pie/pot).
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the idiom in its exact frozen form.
2. Say it aloud with each option; only the original sounds right.
3. Do not pick a 'logical' synonym — idioms do not allow them.

*Why it works:* an idiom is a fixed chain of words, so any substitute breaks it.

example.q: Complete the idiom: *Every cloud has a silver ___.* (a) lining (b) border (c) colour (d) edge
example.solution: The fixed form is *every cloud has a silver lining* = there is some good in every bad situation. Answer: **(a) lining**.

patterns.name: Replace the underlined phrase with an idiom
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a plain-English phrase in bold or underlined; the options are idioms that could replace it.
patterns.logic:
1. Restate the bold phrase in two or three words.
2. Find the option idiom with exactly that meaning.
3. Re-read the sentence with the idiom to check grammar.

*Why it works:* only one option's meaning matches the phrase; the others are real idioms with different meanings.

example.q: Replace the bold part: *The workers **were dismissed from their jobs** last week.* (a) got the sack (b) got cold feet (c) turned the tables (d) broke the ice
example.solution: Dismissed = lost their jobs → **(a) got the sack**.

patterns.name: Mixed-bank idiom meaning (tone check)
patterns.howToSpot: A less familiar idiom from any family, with options of different tones.
patterns.logic:
1. Kill literal options.
2. Judge the idiom's tone from its key word (upper = advantage, dogs = ruin).
3. Pick the option with the same tone and a sensible picture.

*Why it works:* even when memory fails, tone plus picture usually leaves one option.

example.q: Meaning of *To be in the same boat*: (a) to travel together (b) to face the same difficulty (c) to be close friends (d) to share money
example.solution: Everyone in one boat sinks or floats together → shared trouble. Answer: **(b)**.

patterns.name: Opposite in meaning to an idiom
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks for the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the idiom.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the idiom's meaning in two words.
2. Reverse it.
3. Choose that option; reject the option that repeats the meaning.

*Why it works:* the planted trap is the synonym of the idiom's meaning.

example.q: Opposite in meaning to *To be on cloud nine*: (a) to be very happy (b) to be very sad (c) to fly high (d) to be very busy
example.solution: Cloud nine = very happy; opposite = **(b) to be very sad**. (a) is the same meaning, the trap.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One idiom is given on its own and you must choose its meaning from four options. At least one option simply repeats the idiom's words.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cross out every literal option first. Then ask what the picture in the idiom stands for and choose that meaning. Put your answer back into a short sentence to check that it reads naturally.

example.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom: *To throw in the towel*
example.solution: A towel thrown into a boxing ring stops the fight → **to admit defeat and give up**. 'Clean up after a game' is the literal decoy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The idiom is printed in bold inside a sentence, and the options are possible meanings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Decide from the sentence whether the situation is good or bad news. Remove options with the wrong tone, then test the survivors in place of the idiom.

example.q: *The minister's promise **ended in smoke**.* Meaning?
example.solution: A promise that ends in smoke disappears → **came to nothing**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The idiom contains an animal (bull, rat, crocodile, wolf) or a body part (ear, eye, neck, feet, hand).
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the animal's fixed character (crocodile = fake, bull = bold) or the body part's job (ear = listen, neck = risk). This decodes most such idioms even if you only half remember them.

example.q: Meaning of *Crocodile tears*
example.solution: Crocodile = fake → **pretended sorrow**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Colour and food idioms, including look-alike twins
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A colour (red, blue, green, white, black) or a food (cake, nut, potato, apple) appears in the idiom; often one option is the meaning of a twin idiom.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the colour's feeling or the food's judgement. Watch the three reds: see red (angry), red tape (official delay), red-letter day (happy day). Cross out the twin idiom's meaning.

example.q: Meaning of *Red tape*
example.solution: **Too many official rules causing delay**. 'A memorable day' is the twin (red-letter day).

pyqPatterns.pattern: Fill in the blank with an idiom
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a blank and the four options are idioms.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name what the sentence needs (running away, a lower role, a small fuss, a joyful day). Choose the idiom from that family and read the sentence again to check grammar.

example.q: *Seeing the police, the pickpocket ___.* (took to his heels / broke the ice / kept his chin up / turned a deaf ear)
example.solution: The thief escapes → **took to his heels**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A name or story object appears: Achilles, Pandora, Hercules, Midas, a Trojan horse, belling the cat.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the one-line story and turn its key point into a general meaning. Options that retell the story literally are wrong.

example.q: Meaning of *Achilles' heel*
example.solution: The hero could be wounded only at his heel → **a weak point in a strong person or system**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Replace the phrase with an idiom
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Words in a sentence are in bold; the options are idioms that might replace them.
pyqPatterns.approach: Restate the bold words in two or three plain words, then pick the idiom that has exactly that meaning. The other options are real idioms with different meanings.

example.q: *The workers **were dismissed from their jobs**.*
example.solution: Dismissed → **got the sack**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Complete the idiom / opposite of an idiom
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Either one word of a fixed idiom is missing, or the stem asks for the option opposite in meaning.
pyqPatterns.approach: Idioms are frozen, so only the original word completes them (a spade a **spade**). For opposites, write the meaning first, then reverse it; the option that repeats the meaning is the trap.

example.q: Opposite of *To keep one's chin up*
example.solution: Meaning = stay cheerful; opposite = **to lose heart**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A verb with a particle (call off, put up with, give up) is asked for meaning, or a blank follows a verb and the options are up/off/out/down/in.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the particle's idea: off = cancel/stop, out = finish/remove, down = refuse/fail, after = care/resemble, into = investigate. Test each option in the sentence.

example.q: *Our car broke ___ on the highway.*
example.solution: Machines stop working → **down**.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To smell a rat
options: to suspect that something wrong is happening
to suffer from a foul smell
solvedExamples.solution: The picture: a rat hiding somewhere, betrayed by its smell — something hidden and dishonest. Hence **to suspect wrongdoing**. The literal options (foul smell, rodents, dead animal) die on the photograph test, and each can be photographed.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Kill what you can photograph; translate the picture: hidden rat = hidden wrongdoing.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A blessing in disguise
options: a misfortune that turns out to be beneficial
a blessing said in a low voice
solvedExamples.solution: The picture: a blessing that arrived wearing the *disguise* of trouble. The abstract meaning: an apparent misfortune that proves beneficial. Options about gifts, costumes or whispers are literal translations of 'disguise' and die at once.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Split the idiom: blessing = good outcome, in disguise = looked bad first.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To pass the buck
options: to shift responsibility to someone else
solvedExamples.solution: From card-playing: the 'buck' (a marker) showed whose turn to deal; passing it handed the duty to another. Hence **shifting one's responsibility to someone else**. Money and betting options trade on the word 'pass' — both are decoys built on the surface vocabulary.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Allusion anchor: the buck = the marker of responsibility; passing it = escaping duty.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Once in a blue moon
practice.solution: A blue moon (a second full moon in a month) hardly ever occurs → **very rarely**. 'Every month' and 'on a full-moon night' are literal moon options — photographable decoys.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To burn the midnight oil
options: to light lamps for a festival
to set something on fire at night
to work or study late into the night
practice.solution: Before electricity, lamps burned oil; burning it at midnight meant **working late**. The image survives as an idiom for late effort.
practice.shortcut: Picture: oil lamp at midnight → late-night work.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A white elephant
practice.solution: Kings once gifted white elephants whose upkeep ruined the receiver — grand to own, ruinous to keep → **a costly, useless possession**. The sacred/rare options take the colour literally.
practice.shortcut: Upkeep test: does keeping it drain you? That is the white elephant.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To beat about the bush
options: to search carefully in a forest
to avoid coming to the point
practice.solution: Hunters beat *around* bushes to flush game without striking it — skirting the centre. Hence **avoiding the main topic**.
practice.shortcut: Picture: striking the edges, never the centre → dodging the point.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To bite the bullet
options: to endure a painful situation bravely
practice.solution: Soldiers once bit a bullet during surgery without anaesthesia — **to bear pain with courage**. 'To give up easily' inverts the meaning; the rest are literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To turn a deaf ear
practice.solution: The ear that 'turns away' refuses to hear — **deliberate ignoring**, not physical deafness ('hearing loss' is the literal decoy).
practice.shortcut: Body-function logic: ear = listening; turned away = refusing to listen.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

In hot water
practice.solution: Trouble scalds; being 'in hot water' = **in difficulty or disfavour**. Bath, anger and weather options are temperature-literal.
practice.shortcut: Water temperature = trouble scale: hot water = trouble.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To make both ends meet
practice.solution: One's two 'ends' — income and expense — must touch: **to manage on a limited income**. Ropes, tasks and friendships are literal decoys for 'ends'.
practice.shortcut: Ends = income and expense; making them meet = balancing a budget.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Achilles' heel
options: a weak point despite overall strength
practice.solution: The hero Achilles was invulnerable except where his mother held him — his heel. Hence **the one weakness in a strong person or system**.
practice.shortcut: Allusion anchor: the great hero's single vulnerable spot.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To spill the beans
practice.solution: An upturned jar of beans cannot be taken back — the secret is out → **reveal a secret**. Note the sibling idiom 'cry over spilt milk' (vain regret); papers plant one as the other's decoy.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To pull someone's leg
practice.solution: A playful tug at the leg = **to joke at someone's expense**. The tone is friendly — 'to cheat' and 'to injure' overshoot the idiom's mildness.
practice.shortcut: Tone check: the act is a joke, not an attack.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

At the drop of a hat
practice.solution: A dropped hat was the instant signal to begin a fight or race → **immediately, without needing any reason**. 'Reluctance' and 'planning' contradict the idiom's whole point.
practice.shortcut: Signal picture: hat drops, action starts.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To keep the wolf from the door
options: to guard a house at night
to shut the door in anger
practice.solution: The wolf at the door is hunger; keeping it out means **earning barely enough to live**. House-guarding and pet options are literal.
practice.shortcut: Wolf = hunger; keeping it away = basic survival income.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To smell a rat
practice.solution: A hidden rat betrayed by its smell = a hidden deceit betrayed by signs → **to suspect trickery**. 'To detect a thief red-handed' overshoots — smelling a rat is suspicion, not proof.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To hit the nail on the head
options: to state exactly the right thing
practice.solution: One clean, accurate blow — a description or answer perfectly on target → **to speak with exact correctness**.
practice.shortcut: Accuracy picture: the blow lands precisely.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To break the ice
options: to start a conversation among people who feel shy or stiff
to melt ice for drinking water
practice.solution: *Break the ice* = to get people talking and relaxed in a new or awkward group. 'Melt ice' is the literal decoy; the other two have nothing to do with the picture.
practice.shortcut: Ice = stiffness between strangers; breaking it = starting talk.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To throw in the towel
options: to clean up after a game
to admit defeat and give up
practice.solution: In boxing, a towel thrown into the ring stops the fight. So *throw in the towel* = **admit defeat and give up**. The cleaning and clothes options are literal.
practice.shortcut: Towel thrown → fight stops → give up.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To face the music
options: to accept the unpleasant results of one's own actions
practice.solution: *Face the music* = to accept criticism or punishment for what one has done. The concert and loud-music options are literal; 'run away from punishment' is the opposite.
practice.shortcut: Kill the two music options; the opposite is the last trap.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

After failing twice, Ravi decided to **turn over a new leaf** and study every day.
options: to start reading a new book
to start behaving in a better way
practice.solution: The sentence shows Ravi changing his habits after failure. *Turn over a new leaf* = **start a better way of behaving**. Book, tree and school options take 'leaf' literally or guess.
practice.shortcut: Leaf = page of life; a new page = a fresh, better start.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

The minister's promise of free laptops **ended in smoke**.
practice.solution: *End in smoke* = to come to nothing after much talk or effort. 'Caused a fire' is literal; 'kept on time' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

Meena was **on cloud nine** when she cleared the exam.
practice.solution: Clearing an exam is good news, so the meaning must be positive. *On cloud nine* = **extremely happy**.
practice.shortcut: Good-news sentence → pick the only happy option.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To bury the hatchet
options: to hide a weapon in the ground
to make peace after a quarrel
practice.solution: A hatchet (small axe) stands for the fight; burying it ends the fight. So *bury the hatchet* = **make peace**. 'Keep a secret' borrows the idea of burying but not the fight; 'start a quarrel' is the reverse.
practice.shortcut: Weapon put away for ever = peace.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To get cold feet
options: to catch a cold in winter
to become too nervous to do something one had planned
practice.solution: *Get cold feet* = to lose courage just before doing something planned (a speech, a wedding, a jump). Laziness and loneliness are different feelings; the cold option is literal.
practice.shortcut: Feet = courage to step forward; cold feet = courage fails.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To sit on the fence
options: to avoid taking sides in a dispute
practice.solution: A fence divides two fields; sitting on it means not stepping into either. *Sit on the fence* = **avoid taking sides**.
practice.shortcut: On the fence = in neither camp.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To cry over spilt milk
options: to regret something that cannot be undone
practice.solution: *Cry over spilt milk* = to feel useless regret about what is already done. 'Reveal a secret' is the meaning of its look-alike *spill the beans* — the planted twin.
practice.shortcut: Spilt MILK = regret; spill the BEANS = secret.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A bolt from the blue
options: a sudden and completely unexpected event
practice.solution: *A bolt from the blue* = a shock that comes without any warning (like lightning from a clear sky). 'Very rarely' is the meaning of the twin *once in a blue moon*.
practice.shortcut: BOLT = sudden shock; blue MOON = rare.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

The rat race
options: a tiring and endless struggle for success in modern life
to suspect that something is wrong
practice.solution: *The rat race* = the endless competition for money and position, especially in city jobs. 'Suspect that something is wrong' belongs to the twin *smell a rat*.
practice.shortcut: Rat RACE = competition; SMELL a rat = suspicion.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To take the bull by the horns
options: to face a difficult situation boldly
practice.solution: Grabbing a charging bull by its horns means facing the danger directly. Meaning: **deal with a difficulty boldly**. 'Run away' is the opposite; 'tame an animal' is literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Crocodile tears
options: the tears of a wild animal
practice.solution: Crocodiles were believed to shed tears while eating their prey, so the tears were false. *Crocodile tears* = **pretended sorrow**. 'Deep grief' is the opposite (real sorrow).

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To kill two birds with one stone
options: to make two mistakes at once
to achieve two aims with a single action
practice.solution: One stone, two results. Meaning: **get two things done with one effort**. Example: going to the bank on the way to office.
practice.shortcut: Birds = targets; one stone = one action.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To give someone the cold shoulder
options: to treat someone in a deliberately unfriendly way
to push someone away with force
practice.solution: Shoulder = welcome; a cold one = an unfriendly welcome. Meaning: **to ignore or treat someone coldly on purpose**. 'Firm support' confuses it with *a shoulder to lean on*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To pay through the nose
options: to pay one's bills on time
to pay far more than the fair price
practice.solution: *Pay through the nose* = to be charged much too much. Example: buying water at an airport. The breathing option is literal.
practice.shortcut: Nose idiom about money = paying too much.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

The two brothers never **see eye to eye** on money matters.
practice.solution: *See eye to eye* = to agree fully. 'Never see eye to eye' = they always disagree about money. 'Look at each other' is literal.
practice.shortcut: Eye to eye = same view = agreement.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

When the boss asked who would take charge of the failing project, only Anil **stuck his neck out**.
options: took a risk by coming forward boldly
practice.solution: Neck = risk. *Stick one's neck out* = to take a risk by saying or doing something bold. Anil volunteered for a risky job.
practice.shortcut: Neck out = exposed to danger = risk.

practice.q: Select the idiom that means *to be extremely busy*.
practice.solution: *Have one's hands full* = be very busy. *Lend a hand* = help; *wash one's hands of* = refuse further responsibility; *try one's hand at* = attempt something new.
practice.shortcut: Full hands = no free hand = busy.

practice.q: Select the idiom that means *to refuse to take any further responsibility for something*.
practice.solution: *Wash one's hands of* a matter = declare you are no longer responsible for it. *Put one's foot down* = take a firm stand; *keep at arm's length* = avoid closeness; *follow in someone's footsteps* = do as an elder did.
practice.shortcut: Washing hands = removing oneself from the matter.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A black sheep
options: a member who brings disgrace to the family or group
the youngest child in a family
practice.solution: Black = disgrace. *A black sheep* is the member whose conduct shames the family or group.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Green with envy
options: new to a job and inexperienced
practice.solution: Green = envy, so *green with envy* = **very jealous**. 'Inexperienced' is a different use of green (a greenhorn), not this idiom.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To see red
practice.solution: Red = anger here. *See red* = to lose one's temper suddenly. 'Notice danger' treats red as a signal light.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A piece of cake
practice.solution: Cake = easy. *A piece of cake* = a task that needs almost no effort.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A hard nut to crack
options: a difficult problem or a person hard to deal with
practice.solution: Nut = hard to open. *A hard nut to crack* = a problem that is difficult to solve or a person who is difficult to handle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To butter someone up
options: to flatter someone to win a favour
practice.solution: Butter makes things smooth. *Butter someone up* = to praise someone too much so that they will do you a favour.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Red tape
options: too many official rules that cause delay
a ribbon cut at an opening ceremony
practice.solution: Government files were once tied with red tape, and getting them moved was slow. *Red tape* = **official delay caused by rules**. 'A day worth remembering' is the twin *red-letter day*; the ribbon is literal.
practice.shortcut: Red TAPE = delay; red-LETTER day = happy day.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

The apple of one's eye
options: a person who is loved most
practice.solution: *The apple of one's eye* = the person someone loves and cherishes most. 'A cause of quarrel' is the twin *apple of discord*.
practice.shortcut: Apple of EYE = love; apple of DISCORD = quarrel.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A hot potato
options: a sensitive issue that people avoid dealing with
practice.solution: A hot potato is too hot to hold, so everyone passes it on. *A hot potato* = **a touchy issue nobody wants to handle**. 'A very easy task' is the food twin *a piece of cake*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Taking sand to the Thar Desert to sell is like ___.
practice.solution: Newcastle was famous for coal, so taking coal there is pointless. The desert already has endless sand → **carrying coals to Newcastle** = taking something to a place that already has plenty.
practice.shortcut: Place already full of the thing → coals to Newcastle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

The quarrel over the window seat was just ___; the two friends were laughing together five minutes later.
practice.solution: A big fuss over a small matter that ends quickly = **a storm in a teacup**.
practice.shortcut: Big fuss + tiny cause = storm in a teacup.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

The day Priya received her appointment letter was ___ for the whole family.
practice.solution: A joyful, memorable day = **a red-letter day** (special days were marked in red on calendars). The others do not describe a day.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To leave no stone unturned
options: to be careless in one's work
practice.solution: Turning every stone = searching everywhere. *Leave no stone unturned* = **make every possible effort**. 'Careless' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Under the weather
practice.solution: *Under the weather* = feeling a little unwell. The storm option is literal.
practice.shortcut: Health family: under the weather = not well.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To turn the tables
options: to cheat in a game of cards
to reverse a situation and gain the upper hand over an opponent
practice.solution: *Turn the tables* = to change a losing position into a winning one against someone. 'Lose badly' is the opposite; furniture is literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A fair-weather friend
options: a loyal friend in all situations
a friend who stays only in good times
practice.solution: Fair weather = good times. A *fair-weather friend* disappears when trouble comes. 'A loyal friend' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A snake in the grass
options: a hidden enemy who pretends to be a friend
practice.solution: A snake hidden in grass strikes without warning. *A snake in the grass* = **a treacherous person who hides behind friendship**.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A man of straw
options: a person with a strong will
a person of no real importance or strength
practice.solution: Straw is light and weak. *A man of straw* = a weak person with no real substance or power. 'Scarecrow' is literal; 'strong will' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Tired of ___ to his elder brother in the family business, Karan started his own shop.
practice.solution: Karan was unhappy with a lower role → **playing second fiddle** (taking a less important position). The others mean winning, being satisfied with past success, and running away.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Seeing the police van, the pickpocket ___.
practice.solution: A thief who sees the police runs away → **took to his heels** (ran away fast).

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To bell the cat
options: to take a great risk for the good of others
to tie a bell on a pet
practice.solution: In the fable, the mice wanted a bell on the cat but nobody dared to tie it. *Bell the cat* = **to face the danger that others fear, for everyone's benefit**.
practice.shortcut: Fable of the mice → the brave, risky job.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

A Herculean task
options: a task that is very easy
a task that needs very great effort
an order given by a king
practice.solution: Hercules, the hero of Greek stories, did twelve extremely hard labours. *A Herculean task* = **a job needing enormous strength or effort**.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To open Pandora's box
options: to start something that causes many unexpected problems
to open a box of gifts
practice.solution: In the Greek story, Pandora opened a forbidden box and let all kinds of troubles into the world. *Open Pandora's box* = **start something that leads to many new problems**.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate word to complete the idiom.

Rahul does not believe in hiding the truth; he always calls a spade a ___.
practice.solution: The fixed idiom is *call a spade a spade* = to speak plainly and honestly. Idioms are frozen: 'a spade a shovel' is not the idiom.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate word to complete the idiom.

The new supervisor likes to have a finger in every ___.
practice.solution: The fixed idiom is *have a finger in every pie* = to be involved in (or meddle in) many matters.
practice.shortcut: Recall the frozen chain: finger → every pie.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate word to complete the idiom.

Don't count your chickens before they ___; the result is not out yet.
practice.solution: The fixed idiom is *don't count your chickens before they hatch* = don't depend on a gain before it is certain.

practice.q:
Select the idiom that can replace the words in bold.

The two neighbours have been **openly and bitterly hostile to each other** for years.
practice.solution: *At daggers drawn* = in open, bitter enmity. *At sixes and sevens* = in confusion; *on cloud nine* = very happy; *at a loose end* = having nothing to do.

practice.q:
Select the option that can replace the words in bold.

Priya **always speaks plainly, without softening her words**.
practice.solution: *Not mince matters (or words)* = to speak frankly without softening. *Beat about the bush* is the opposite; *sit on the fence* = avoid taking sides; *pull one's weight* = do one's fair share of work.
practice.shortcut: Mince = cut small = soften; never mince = speak plainly.

practice.q:
Select the idiom that can replace the words in bold.

In the final debate, Aman's argument **won and was accepted by everyone**.
practice.solution: *Carry the day* = to win or be successful. *Fall flat* = fail to have the intended effect; *miss the bus* = lose an opportunity; *go to the dogs* = be ruined.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To have the upper hand
options: to raise one's hand to ask
to be in a weak position
to have control or an advantage
practice.solution: Upper = above the other. *Have the upper hand* = to be in control or in a stronger position. 'Weak position' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

At sixes and sevens
practice.solution: *At sixes and sevens* = in a state of confusion or disorder. The number options are literal; 'perfect order' is the opposite.
practice.shortcut: Numbers in an idiom are never literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To go to the dogs
options: to be ruined or become much worse
to go for a morning walk
practice.solution: *Go to the dogs* = to decline badly or be ruined (a business, a person, a place). 'Improve greatly' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the option that is OPPOSITE in meaning to the given idiom.

To keep one's chin up
practice.solution: *Keep one's chin up* = stay brave and cheerful in hard times. Its opposite is **to lose heart**. 'Stay cheerful' is the same meaning (the trap).
practice.shortcut: Write the meaning (stay brave), then reverse it.

practice.q:
Select the option that is OPPOSITE in meaning to the given idiom.

To blow hot and cold
options: to hold the same opinion firmly
practice.solution: *Blow hot and cold* = to keep changing one's mind, to be unsteady. Opposite: **to hold one opinion firmly**. 'Keep changing one's opinion' is the same meaning.
practice.shortcut: Hot then cold = changing; opposite = steady.

practice.q:
Select the option that is OPPOSITE in meaning to the given idiom.

To be in someone's good books
options: to be out of favour with someone
practice.solution: *Be in someone's good books* = to be in their favour. Opposite: **out of favour** with them. 'Liked by someone' repeats the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

To call off
practice.solution: *Call off* = cancel: *The match was called off because of rain.* The phone and shouting options use the plain verb *call*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

To put up with
practice.solution: *Put up with* = to bear or tolerate something unpleasant: *I cannot put up with this noise.*

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

To look down upon
practice.solution: *Look down upon* = to think that someone is less important than oneself. 'Respect' is the opposite; 'from a height' is literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

We have run ___ of sugar; please buy some on your way home.
practice.solution: *Run out of* = to have no more left. Only *out* forms this phrase with *of*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Our car broke ___ on the highway, so we had to wait for a mechanic.
practice.solution: A machine that stops working *breaks down*. *Break out* is for war, fire or disease; *break up* ends a relationship; *break in* is forced entry.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The police have promised to look ___ the complaint and find out the truth.
practice.solution: *Look into* = to investigate. 'Find out the truth' confirms investigation.

practice.q: Select the phrasal verb that means *to stop a habit*.
practice.solution: *Give up* smoking = stop the habit. *Give in* = surrender; *give out* = distribute or stop working; *give away* = donate or reveal.

practice.q: Select the phrasal verb that means *to refuse an offer or request*.
practice.solution: *Turn down* an offer = refuse it. *Turn up* = arrive; *turn out* = prove to be; *turn over* = flip, or hand over.

practice.q: Select the phrasal verb that means *to look or behave like an older family member*.
practice.solution: *She takes after her mother* = she resembles her mother. *Take off* = remove or leave the ground; *take up* = start a hobby or job; *take in* = deceive or absorb.

practice.q:
Select the phrasal verb that can replace the word in bold.

The fire brigade managed to **extinguish** the fire within an hour.
practice.solution: *Put out* a fire = extinguish it. *Put off* = postpone; *put on* = wear or switch on; *put up* = raise or stay.

practice.q:
Select the phrasal verb that can replace the words in bold.

My grandfather **recovered from** his illness quickly.
practice.solution: *Get over* an illness = recover from it. *Get through* = pass or finish; *get along* = be friendly with; *get off* = leave a bus or escape punishment.

practice.q:
Select the phrasal verb that can replace the words in bold.

Ramesh **happened to meet** an old school friend at the railway station.
practice.solution: *Come across* = meet or find by chance. *Come about* = happen; *come off* = succeed or become detached; *come out* = appear or be published.
